source.title: Bayesian Deep Learning and a Probabilistic Perspective of Generalization

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendix; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests the random-label/generalization coexistence in V1 using Gaussian processes and Bayesian neural networks, and tests width-dependent double descent in V2 using Bayesian marginalization. These are conceptual tests with different models or measures from the versions’ specified original recipes.
record.gate_note: Other discussion of architecture, optimizer, batches, dropout, sharpness, and memorized-example removal is cited prior work, not a result of this study. The study's own width-sweep results concern double descent and Bayesian marginalization; they do not directly test V2's claim that unregularized one-hidden-layer ReLU networks keep lowering test error past interpolation.
record.test_reason: The study measures random-label fitting in PreResNet-20 and width-dependent test error in ResNet-18, extending parts of V1 and V2 to new architectures and recipes. Its Gaussian-process experiments reproduce a related pattern in a different kind of system.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors distinguish model support from inductive bias, reproduce the memorization/generalization pattern with Gaussian processes, and find decreasing approximate marginal likelihood with label corruption. They report that MultiSWAG removes double descent in their width sweeps and improves accuracy and NLL over SGD and SWAG.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Gaussian-process classification and Bayesian neural-network marginal likelihood for random-label results, plus ResNet-18 width sweeps with SGD, SWAG, and MultiSWAG for double descent. This differs from the listed original unregularized networks and one-hidden-layer ReLU width sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: For width-dependent results, the outcome changes by inference method: SGD shows double descent, SWAG reduces it but still shows it under 20% label corruption, and MultiSWAG removes it. Label corruption is also varied.

fits_no_version.finding: RBF Gaussian processes fit random-label CIFAR-10 at 100% training accuracy and 10.4% test accuracy, while natural-label test accuracy is 54.3%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization can coexist in Gaussian-process classifiers.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing the number of independent SWAG approximations lowers ensemble test error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Marginalizing more independently trained modes improves MultiSWAG classification performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Width and marginalization method affect held-out negative log likelihood and its double-descent pattern.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multimodal Bayesian averaging can remove width-dependent double descent in predictive log loss.

record.problems: The random-label neural-network result is limited to training accuracy and marginal-likelihood trends; the paper does not report held-out accuracy for its corrupted-label PreResNet condition. The width-sweep values are presented in figures without numeric text values or reported uncertainty. The double-descent experiments use ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 and do not test the one-hidden-layer ReLU setup specified in V2.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying result rows omitted. Figure 7's marginal-likelihood trends are described as support for the prior but do not directly measure the versions' named training/test accuracy behavior. The true-label and random-label GP accuracy results and width-sweep results are included above.

untested.parts: The named original architectures are not tested. The recorded neural-network accuracy row establishes random-label fitting, but not the complete paired natural-label and random-label held-out pattern.
One-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10, convergence without explicit regularization, and the width reaching zero training error are not established here.
No trained convolutional-versus-fully-connected test-error comparison or learned-locality intervention.
No magnitude-aware sharpness ranking against generalization gaps.

missing.what: PreResNet-20 test-error results across label-corruption levels, including natural and fully corrupted labels. Figure 7(e) includes a test-error curve, but its values cannot be recovered from the supplied text extraction.
Width-dependent classification error with 10% label corruption for SGD, SWAG and MultiSWAG. The caption reports alleviation of double descent by MultiSWAG; separate method rows are needed.
Deep ensembles also mitigate double descent under 20% corruption, with accuracy approximately 1–2 percentage points worse than MultiSWAG.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text does not preserve plotted curves well enough for numerical transcription. Double descent's interpolation peak is explicitly separate from V2's post-interpolation claim, so its presence does not justify the record's limits_scope verdict. Differences in architecture or recipe alone are untested scope, not adverse results.

versions.untested_parts: The specified small Inception, AlexNet, MLP, and Inception V3 settings are not tested; no random-label held-out result for a neural network is reported. The GP CIFAR-10 random-label condition is tested, as is the true-label GP comparison.

The specified one-hidden-layer ReLU networks trained without explicit regularization are not tested. Width is varied for ResNet-18 with SGD, SWAG, and MultiSWAG; Bayesian model averaging and label-corruption conditions are also included.
No controlled comparison of convolutional and fully connected image classifiers is reported.
No optimizer generalization comparison between adaptive methods and SGD is reported.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets is reported.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measure is compared with generalization gaps.
No memorized-example removal experiment is reported.

rows.subject: Gaussian processes with RBF kernel
rows.operation_detail: Fit a Gaussian process classifier to CIFAR-10 images with random labels.
rows.note: The paper reports perfect training accuracy for the random-label GP condition.
rows.check: The reported 100% training accuracy is correct, but a Gaussian process does not test V1's neural-network claim.

rows.subject: Gaussian processes with RBF kernel
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate held-out accuracy after fitting CIFAR-10 images with random labels.
rows.note: The text identifies this as the level of random guessing.
rows.check: The reported 10.4% test accuracy is correct, but the subject is a Gaussian process. Nominal chance for ten classes is 10%; 10.4% is the observed result.

rows.subject: Gaussian processes with RBF kernel
rows.operation_detail: Fit a Gaussian process classifier to CIFAR-10 images with true labels.
rows.note: Natural-label training accuracy is reported, but the version's held-out generalization claim is measured by test accuracy.
rows.check: The reported 72.8% training accuracy concerns a Gaussian process, outside V1's neural-network scope.

rows.subject: Gaussian processes with RBF kernel
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate held-out accuracy after fitting CIFAR-10 images with true labels.
rows.note: Same GP model family as the random-label comparison; the reported natural-label test accuracy is far above chance.
rows.check: The reported 54.3% test accuracy concerns a Gaussian process, outside V1's neural-network scope. Nominal chance is 10%.

rows.subject: PreResNet-20
rows.operation_detail: Fit CIFAR-10 with varying fractions of random labels; assess fit and estimate marginal likelihood.

conditions.value: weight decay and data augmentation turned off
marginal likelihood by diagonal Laplace approximation

rows.measure: Training accuracy on fully corrupted labels
rows.note: The study reports 100% training accuracy for fully corrupted labels but does not report held-out accuracy for this neural-network condition.
rows.check: Correct for V1's random-label fitting component: Figure 7 reports 100% training accuracy with fully corrupted labels. This row alone cannot establish coexistence with natural-label generalization. Figure 7(e) also plots test error, contrary to the record's blanket statement that no neural-network held-out result is reported.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Vary network width and evaluate test error for SGD-trained models.
rows.note: The text says SGD models suffer double descent, especially under partially corrupted labels; exact true-label values are only in the figure.
rows.check: Section 7 explicitly reports double descent for SGD, which includes decreasing error on the wider branch. Exact values and the width achieving zero training error are not supplied in readable text; the interpolation peak itself does not contradict V2.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Vary network width and evaluate test error under 20% random label corruption.
rows.note: The authors explicitly describe double descent for SGD, including under label corruption; the figure has no numeric text values.
rows.check: The authors explicitly report double descent under label corruption, including improvement on its wider branch. Exact values and the zero-training-error threshold are not established by the supplied text.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Vary network width and evaluate test error using SWAG.
rows.note: Authors state SWAG reduces double descent; exact values are only in the figure.
rows.check: The text says SWAG reduces double descent but does not separately specify the true-label test-error trend beyond interpolation. The extracted figure does not preserve readable curves.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Vary network width and evaluate test error using SWAG under label corruption.
rows.note: Authors explicitly state SWAG suffers from double descent under 20% label corruption; exact values are only in the figure.
rows.check: Section 7 explicitly identifies double descent for SWAG under 20% corruption, including the wider decreasing branch. Its peak is not evidence against V2's post-interpolation claim.

source_check.locator_found: Section 7 explicitly identifies SWAG double descent under 20% corruption; Figure 8(c); Appendix D.5.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Vary network width and evaluate test error using MultiSWAG, marginalizing multiple modes.
rows.note: Authors state MultiSWAG performance increases monotonically with model size, without double descent; exact values are only in the figure.
rows.check: The authors explicitly report monotonically improving accuracy with width. The relevant baseline is narrower MultiSWAG models, rather than SGD or SWAG. This is a Bayesian ensemble recipe, not the original unregularized single-network recipe.

source_check.correct: For the width-scaling effect, compare wider MultiSWAG models with narrower MultiSWAG models; no numerical baseline is stated. SGD and SWAG are separate cross-method comparators.
source_check.locator_found: Section 7, paragraph reporting monotonic improvement with model size; Figure 8(a); Appendix D.5.
source_check.problem: The baseline names a method comparison rather than the within-MultiSWAG width comparison measured by this row.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Vary network width and evaluate test error using MultiSWAG under label corruption.
rows.note: Authors state MultiSWAG entirely alleviates double descent under significant label corruption; exact values are only in the figure.
rows.check: The authors explicitly report monotonically improving accuracy with width under 20% corruption. Compare against narrower MultiSWAG models. Ten independent SWAG approximations, each contributing 20 sampled networks, are used.

source_check.correct: For the width-scaling effect under 20% corruption, compare wider MultiSWAG models with narrower MultiSWAG models; no numerical baseline is stated. SGD and SWAG are separate cross-method comparators.
source_check.problem: The baseline names a method comparison rather than the within-MultiSWAG width comparison measured by this row.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Vary the number of independent SWAG modes marginalized by MultiSWAG under 20% label corruption.
rows.note: The paper says test error monotonically decreases with increased number of independent models; exact values are figure-only.
rows.check: Increasing the number of independently trained ensemble members is a different intervention from widening a network. A separate width comparison would require its own clearly specified condition.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Vary network width and evaluate NLL using MultiSWAG, marginalizing multiple modes.
rows.note: Authors state MultiSWAG monotonically improves with model size and provides significant NLL improvements over SGD and SWAG.
rows.check: Negative log likelihood is not V2's test-error measure; it can improve through confidence changes without fewer classification mistakes.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Vary network width and evaluate NLL using MultiSWAG under label corruption.
rows.note: Authors state MultiSWAG entirely alleviates double descent under label corruption for NLL as well as accuracy.
rows.check: Negative log likelihood does not directly measure V2's classification-error effect.
